                    - text: ).
                - heading "4.2. Radial Population of Filaments PA in the Galactic Plane" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                - generic [ref=e702]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e703]:
                    - text: The most interesting result of our study is the discovery of a new population of short filaments’ PA that is found along the Galactic plane only at
                    - emphasis [ref=e704]: l
                    - text: < 0°. There is statistical evidence that short filaments PA point toward Sgr A* with the cone in which the filaments are found has FWHM ∼ 20°, but the deviations of filament directions from radial is much broader, over a large scale of ∼300 pc from Sgr A* at
                    - emphasis [ref=e705]: l
                    - text: < 0°. This large-scale anisotropy in the filaments PA is interpreted in the context of a large-scale collimated outflow from Sgr A* along the plane. A wind- or jet-driven outflow from Sgr A* has been suggested to explain evidence for outflow in the plane of the Galaxy within a few arcminutes of Sgr A*.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: There are eight different spectroscopic, polarimetric, and broadband continuum measurements over a wide range of angular scales extending from ∼0.02 to ∼25 pc from Sgr A* that have inferred a jet-driven outflow along the Galactic plane (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2012" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - text: ","
                    - link "2020" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                    - text: and references therein). In this picture the jet emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow and is aligned roughly east−west in Galactic coordinates. A schematic diagram in Figure
                    - link "8" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bf8"
                    - text: showing the interaction of the outflow from Sgr A* with filaments of ionized and molecular gas being aligned roughly along the Galactic flow. For example, blue- and redshifted features in radio recombination line observations on a scale within 14″ (0.56 pc) of Sgr A* invoke an interpretation in terms of the interaction of a collimated outflow driven outflow from Sgr A* along ∼ ± 30° of the Galactic plane (Royster et al.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

                  - text: ). These observations indicate that cosmic-ray pressure in the CMZ is significant when compared to the interstellar gas pressure of the GC.
                - paragraph [ref=e255]:
                  - text: Recent MeerKAT observations have provided a remarkable mosaic of the inner few degrees of the GC with exquisite details at 4″–6″ spatial resolution (Heywood et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: ","

                  - text: ). Statistical properties of the population of GC filaments such as morphology, mean spectral index, equipartition magnetic field, filament spacing and filament association with stellar candidates have recently been studied in detail in a series of papers (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022b" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib38"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022c" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib40"
                  - text: ). VLA observations showed the bright and long filaments emitting nonthermal emission, whereas MeerKAT data showed a great deal of fainter filaments and filamentary structures that are shorter. MeerKAT has also surveyed a large number of galaxy clusters, some of which show exceptional isolated filamentary structures in the intracluster medium (ICM). These filaments appear to be linked to radio jets, tails, and lobes of radio galaxies (Shimwell et al.
                  - link "2016" [ref=e261] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib30"
                  - text: ; Ramatsoku et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib24"
                  - text: ; Condon et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e263] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib5"
                  - text: ; Rudnick et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib27"
                  - text: ). For the first time, a population of magnetized ICM filaments, with an underlying physical mechanism similar to that of the GC filament population, is identified in external galaxies (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022d" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib39"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e266]:
                  - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA). This physical characteristic could potentially provide additional insight into the origin of the enigmatic GC filaments. Previous VLA observations of the brightest GC filaments showed that they are mainly oriented perpendicular to the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib41"
                  - text: and references therein). Using the high sensitivity of MeerKAT data, we examine statistical properties of the PA of the GC filament population. We present evidence that short filaments located on the negative Galactic longitudes have PAs that run mainly within ±20° of the Galactic plane. An extension of the filament PAs show radial distribution, pointing in the direction toward Sgr A* at the GC. The orientation of a large number of filaments within a few hundred parsecs of Sgr A* is similar to those found in radio continuum and recombination line images of the inner few arcminutes of Sgr A* (Royster et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                  - text: ). In addition, ALMA observations of the Sgr E molecular cloud shows parallel filamentary structure along the Galactic plane (Wallace et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                  - text: ). Here we consider a picture in which a collimated outflow, most likely arising from Sgr A*, is responsible for distorting and aligning the shape of molecular, thermal, and nonthermal features along the Galactic plane.

              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively. The vertical and horizontal filaments are characterized to have nonthermal and thermal properties (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ), respectively, based on their spectral indices. While there is clearly an overlap in their properties (e.g., PA, spectral index) a key question is the origin of the bimodal PA distribution of GC filaments.
                - heading "4.1. Vertical Population of Galactic Center Filaments PA" [level=3] [ref=e682]
                - generic [ref=e683]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e684]:
                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north. The negative and positive PAs tend to be found in positive and negative Galactic longitudes, respectively. There is a slightly reduced number of filaments at PAs ∼ 0°, giving roughly a bimodal distribution in the histogram. We also note that vertical filaments dominated by long filaments
                    - emphasis [ref=e685]: L
                    - text: "> 66″ have nonthermal spectra. Considering global distribution of vertical filament PAs, there is no evidence that the extension of all filaments PA converge toward Sgr A* or any other compact sources. This suggests that the creation of roughly symmetric PA distribution is in the Galactic plane within a degree of Sgr A*. This is consistent with a trend noticed in the spectral index of nonthermal filaments as they become steeper with increasing absolute Galactic latitude (Yusef-Zadeh et al."
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ). If synchrotron aging is responsible for the steepening of the spectrum, it implies that the vertical filaments are powered in the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e688]:
                    - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from
                    - text: measurements (e.g., Geballe et al.
                    - link "1999" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib7"
                    - text: ; Oka et al.
                    - link "2005" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib21"
                    - text: ; Oka & Geballe
                    - link "2020" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). The nonthermal radio filaments result from the interaction of the large-scale wind and obstacles embedded within the flow, creating the filaments by wrapping the wind’s magnetic field around the obstacles (Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). However, there are alternate models explaining the origin of the vertical filaments (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ; Sofue
                    - link "2023" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib31"
                    - text: and references therein). This begs the question of the origin of the high cosmic-ray pressure, which is usually attributed to the explosive event a few million years ago that created Fermi bubbles and the bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e699] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - text: ).
                - heading "4.2. Radial Population of Filaments PA in the Galactic Plane" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                - generic [ref=e702]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e703]:
                    - text: The most interesting result of our study is the discovery of a new population of short filaments’ PA that is found along the Galactic plane only at
                    - emphasis [ref=e704]: l
                    - text: < 0°. There is statistical evidence that short filaments PA point toward Sgr A* with the cone in which the filaments are found has FWHM ∼ 20°, but the deviations of filament directions from radial is much broader, over a large scale of ∼300 pc from Sgr A* at
                    - emphasis [ref=e705]: l
                    - text: < 0°. This large-scale anisotropy in the filaments PA is interpreted in the context of a large-scale collimated outflow from Sgr A* along the plane. A wind- or jet-driven outflow from Sgr A* has been suggested to explain evidence for outflow in the plane of the Galaxy within a few arcminutes of Sgr A*.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: There are eight different spectroscopic, polarimetric, and broadband continuum measurements over a wide range of angular scales extending from ∼0.02 to ∼25 pc from Sgr A* that have inferred a jet-driven outflow along the Galactic plane (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2012" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - text: ","
                    - link "2020" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                    - text: and references therein). In this picture the jet emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow and is aligned roughly east−west in Galactic coordinates. A schematic diagram in Figure
                    - link "8" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bf8"
                    - text: showing the interaction of the outflow from Sgr A* with filaments of ionized and molecular gas being aligned roughly along the Galactic flow. For example, blue- and redshifted features in radio recombination line observations on a scale within 14″ (0.56 pc) of Sgr A* invoke an interpretation in terms of the interaction of a collimated outflow driven outflow from Sgr A* along ∼ ± 30° of the Galactic plane (Royster et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e710] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"

                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north.                     - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from

                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.

                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: The prototype magnetized radio filaments in the Galactic center (GC) were discovered close to 40 years ago (Yusef-Zadeh et al.

                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib42"
                  - text: ). Since then, Very Large Array (VLA), Nobeyama 45m-telescope, Mologlo, and ATCA observations have shown linearly polarized synchrotron emission tracing nucleus-wide cosmic-ray activity throughout the inner few hundred parsecs of the Galaxy (Liszt

                  - link "2019" [ref=e218] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: ). Chandra, XMM-Newton (XMM), and NuSTAR have also detected X-ray emission from a handful of nonthermal radio filaments. (Lu et al.

                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e224] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib45"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e225]:
                  - text: High-temperature molecular clouds with large, turbulent line widths also characterize this region, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Furthermore,
                  - generic [ref=e228]:
                    - generic [ref=e230]:
                      - generic [ref=e235]: H
                      - generic [ref=e236]:
                        - generic [ref=e239]: +

                  - text: absorption line observations show that high cosmic-ray ionization rates permeate the CMZ at levels 1000 times that of the solar neighborhood (Oka & Geballe
                  - link "2020" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                  - text: ). These observations indicate that cosmic-ray pressure in the CMZ is significant when compared to the interstellar gas pressure of the GC.
                - paragraph [ref=e255]:
                  - text: Recent MeerKAT observations have provided a remarkable mosaic of the inner few degrees of the GC with exquisite details at 4″–6″ spatial resolution (Heywood et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib11"
                  - text: ). Statistical properties of the population of GC filaments such as morphology, mean spectral index, equipartition magnetic field, filament spacing and filament association with stellar candidates have recently been studied in detail in a series of papers (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022b" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib38"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022c" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib40"
                  - text: ). VLA observations showed the bright and long filaments emitting nonthermal emission, whereas MeerKAT data showed a great deal of fainter filaments and filamentary structures that are shorter. MeerKAT has also surveyed a large number of galaxy clusters, some of which show exceptional isolated filamentary structures in the intracluster medium (ICM). These filaments appear to be linked to radio jets, tails, and lobes of radio galaxies (Shimwell et al.
                  - link "2016" [ref=e261] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib30"
                  - text: ; Ramatsoku et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib24"
                  - text: ; Condon et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e263] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib5"
                  - text: ; Rudnick et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib27"
                  - text: ). For the first time, a population of magnetized ICM filaments, with an underlying physical mechanism similar to that of the GC filament population, is identified in external galaxies (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022d" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib39"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e266]:
                  - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA). This physical characteristic could potentially provide additional insight into the origin of the enigmatic GC filaments. Previous VLA observations of the brightest GC filaments showed that they are mainly oriented perpendicular to the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib41"
                  - text: and references therein). Using the high sensitivity of MeerKAT data, we examine statistical properties of the PA of the GC filament population. We present evidence that short filaments located on the negative Galactic longitudes have PAs that run mainly within ±20° of the Galactic plane. An extension of the filament PAs show radial distribution, pointing in the direction toward Sgr A* at the GC. The orientation of a large number of filaments within a few hundred parsecs of Sgr A* is similar to those found in radio continuum and recombination line images of the inner few arcminutes of Sgr A* (Royster et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                  - text: ). In addition, ALMA observations of the Sgr E molecular cloud shows parallel filamentary structure along the Galactic plane (Wallace et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                  - text: ). Here we consider a picture in which a collimated outflow, most likely arising from Sgr A*, is responsible for distorting and aligning the shape of molecular, thermal, and nonthermal features along the Galactic plane.

                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations.                   - text: ; Staguhn et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e218] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib33"
                  - text: ). Chandra, XMM-Newton (XMM), and NuSTAR have also detected X-ray emission from a handful of nonthermal radio filaments. (Lu et al.
                  - link "2003" [ref=e219] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib18"
                  - text: ; Sakano et al.
                  - link "2003" [ref=e220] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib28"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2005" [ref=e221] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib46"
                  - text: ; Zhang et al.
                  - link "2014" [ref=e222] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib47"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2020" [ref=e223] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib48"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e224] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib45"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e225]:
                  - text: High-temperature molecular clouds with large, turbulent line widths also characterize this region, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Furthermore,
                  - generic [ref=e228]:
                    - generic [ref=e230]:
                      - generic [ref=e235]: H
                      - generic [ref=e236]:
                        - generic [ref=e239]: +
                        - generic [ref=e242]: "3"
                    - math [ref=e244]:
                      - generic [ref=e245]:
                        - generic [ref=e249]: H
                        - generic [ref=e251]: "3"
                        - generic [ref=e253]: +
                  - text: absorption line observations show that high cosmic-ray ionization rates permeate the CMZ at levels 1000 times that of the solar neighborhood (Oka & Geballe
                  - link "2020" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                  - text: ). These observations indicate that cosmic-ray pressure in the CMZ is significant when compared to the interstellar gas pressure of the GC.
                - paragraph [ref=e255]:
                  - text: Recent MeerKAT observations have provided a remarkable mosaic of the inner few degrees of the GC with exquisite details at 4″–6″ spatial resolution (Heywood et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib11"
                  - text: ). Statistical properties of the population of GC filaments such as morphology, mean spectral index, equipartition magnetic field, filament spacing and filament association with stellar candidates have recently been studied in detail in a series of papers (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022b" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib38"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022c" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib40"
                  - text: ). VLA observations showed the bright and long filaments emitting nonthermal emission, whereas MeerKAT data showed a great deal of fainter filaments and filamentary structures that are shorter. MeerKAT has also surveyed a large number of galaxy clusters, some of which show exceptional isolated filamentary structures in the intracluster medium (ICM). These filaments appear to be linked to radio jets, tails, and lobes of radio galaxies (Shimwell et al.
                  - link "2016" [ref=e261] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib30"
                  - text: ; Ramatsoku et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib24"
                  - text: ; Condon et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e263] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib5"
                  - text: ; Rudnick et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib27"
                  - text: ). For the first time, a population of magnetized ICM filaments, with an underlying physical mechanism similar to that of the GC filament population, is identified in external galaxies (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022d" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib39"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e266]:
                  - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA). This physical characteristic could potentially provide additional insight into the origin of the enigmatic GC filaments. Previous VLA observations of the brightest GC filaments showed that they are mainly oriented perpendicular to the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib41"
                  - text: and references therein). Using the high sensitivity of MeerKAT data, we examine statistical properties of the PA of the GC filament population. We present evidence that short filaments located on the negative Galactic longitudes have PAs that run mainly within ±20° of the Galactic plane. An extension of the filament PAs show radial distribution, pointing in the direction toward Sgr A* at the GC. The orientation of a large number of filaments within a few hundred parsecs of Sgr A* is similar to those found in radio continuum and recombination line images of the inner few arcminutes of Sgr A* (Royster et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                  - text: ). In addition, ALMA observations of the Sgr E molecular cloud shows parallel filamentary structure along the Galactic plane (Wallace et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                  - text: ). Here we consider a picture in which a collimated outflow, most likely arising from Sgr A*, is responsible for distorting and aligning the shape of molecular, thermal, and nonthermal features along the Galactic plane.

              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively. The vertical and horizontal filaments are characterized to have nonthermal and thermal properties (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ), respectively, based on their spectral indices. While there is clearly an overlap in their properties (e.g., PA, spectral index) a key question is the origin of the bimodal PA distribution of GC filaments.
                - heading "4.1. Vertical Population of Galactic Center Filaments PA" [level=3] [ref=e682]
                - generic [ref=e683]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e684]:
                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north. The negative and positive PAs tend to be found in positive and negative Galactic longitudes, respectively. There is a slightly reduced number of filaments at PAs ∼ 0°, giving roughly a bimodal distribution in the histogram. We also note that vertical filaments dominated by long filaments
                    - emphasis [ref=e685]: L
                    - text: "> 66″ have nonthermal spectra. Considering global distribution of vertical filament PAs, there is no evidence that the extension of all filaments PA converge toward Sgr A* or any other compact sources. This suggests that the creation of roughly symmetric PA distribution is in the Galactic plane within a degree of Sgr A*. This is consistent with a trend noticed in the spectral index of nonthermal filaments as they become steeper with increasing absolute Galactic latitude (Yusef-Zadeh et al."
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ). If synchrotron aging is responsible for the steepening of the spectrum, it implies that the vertical filaments are powered in the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e688]:
                    - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from
                    - text: measurements (e.g., Geballe et al.
                    - link "1999" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib7"
                    - text: ; Oka et al.
                    - link "2005" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib21"
                    - text: ; Oka & Geballe
                    - link "2020" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). The nonthermal radio filaments result from the interaction of the large-scale wind and obstacles embedded within the flow, creating the filaments by wrapping the wind’s magnetic field around the obstacles (Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). However, there are alternate models explaining the origin of the vertical filaments (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.

                    - text: ; Sofue

                    - text: and references therein). This begs the question of the origin of the high cosmic-ray pressure, which is usually attributed to the explosive event a few million years ago that created Fermi bubbles and the bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:

              - heading "Abstract" [level=2] [ref=e168]
              - paragraph [ref=e170]:
                - text: We have examined the distribution of the position angle (PA) of the Galactic center filaments with lengths L > 66″ and <66″ as well as their length distribution as a function of PA. We find bimodal PA distributions of the filaments, and long and short populations of radio filaments. Our PA study shows the evidence for a distinct population of short filaments with PA close to the Galactic plane. Mainly thermal, short-radio filaments (<66″) have PAs concentrated close to the Galactic plane within 60° < PA < 120°. Remarkably, the short filament PAs are radial with respect to the Galactic center at l < 0° and extend in the direction toward Sgr A*. On a smaller scale, the prominent Sgr E H ii complex G358.7-0.0 provides a vivid example of the nearly radial distribution of short filaments. The bimodal PA distribution suggests a different origin for two distinct filament populations. We argue that the alignment of the short-filament population results from the ram pressure of a degree-scale outflow from Sgr A* that exceeds the internal filament pressure, and aligns them along the Galactic plane. The ram pressure is estimated to be 2 × 10

                - paragraph [ref=e266]:
                  - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA).                   - link "2004" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - paragraph [ref=e658]:
                      - text: This pattern of radial structure close to the Galactic plane is seen on even small-scale observations of some of the compact molecular clouds in the region. Recent ALMA observations of CO associated with the Sgr E complex finds two molecular filaments running close to the Galactic plane within ALMA’s 52″ field of view. These molecular filaments have an aspect ratio of ∼5 to 1 and show alignment within 2° of the Galactic plane (Wallace et al.
                      - link "2022" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                      - text: ) and appear to align radially toward the GC. The origin of this filamentary structure is suggested to be due to stretching of the Sgr E cloud by the gravitational field of the Galactic bar potential. The PAs of the CO filaments resemble those found in our radio continuum study, so it is possible that they are produced by the mechanism responsible for aligning the radio filaments. MeerKAT radio image shows a short filament G358.712 + 0.027 with an extent of ∼1′ and a PA of 106° (a deviation of 15° from a radial orientation), possibly associated with the molecular filament.

                    - paragraph [ref=e676]:
                      - text: The dark feature in the continuum MeerKAT and GBT images is anticorrelated with the Sgr E CO cloud. This dark feature shows similar appearance to many GC molecular clouds that have been identified as radio dark clouds (Yusef-Zadeh

              - heading "4. Discussion" [level=2] [ref=e678]
              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively. The vertical and horizontal filaments are characterized to have nonthermal and thermal properties (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ), respectively, based on their spectral indices. While there is clearly an overlap in their properties (e.g., PA, spectral index) a key question is the origin of the bimodal PA distribution of GC filaments.
                - heading "4.1. Vertical Population of Galactic Center Filaments PA" [level=3] [ref=e682]
                - generic [ref=e683]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e684]:
                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north. The negative and positive PAs tend to be found in positive and negative Galactic longitudes, respectively. There is a slightly reduced number of filaments at PAs ∼ 0°, giving roughly a bimodal distribution in the histogram. We also note that vertical filaments dominated by long filaments
                    - emphasis [ref=e685]: L
                    - text: "> 66″ have nonthermal spectra. Considering global distribution of vertical filament PAs, there is no evidence that the extension of all filaments PA converge toward Sgr A* or any other compact sources. This suggests that the creation of roughly symmetric PA distribution is in the Galactic plane within a degree of Sgr A*. This is consistent with a trend noticed in the spectral index of nonthermal filaments as they become steeper with increasing absolute Galactic latitude (Yusef-Zadeh et al."
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ). If synchrotron aging is responsible for the steepening of the spectrum, it implies that the vertical filaments are powered in the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e688]:
                    - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from
                    - text: measurements (e.g., Geballe et al.
                    - link "1999" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib7"
                    - text: ; Oka et al.
                    - link "2005" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib21"
                    - text: ; Oka & Geballe
                    - link "2020" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). The nonthermal radio filaments result from the interaction of the large-scale wind and obstacles embedded within the flow, creating the filaments by wrapping the wind’s magnetic field around the obstacles (Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). However, there are alternate models explaining the origin of the vertical filaments (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ; Sofue
                    - link "2023" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib31"
                    - text: and references therein). This begs the question of the origin of the high cosmic-ray pressure, which is usually attributed to the explosive event a few million years ago that created Fermi bubbles and the bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e699] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ).
                - heading "4.2. Radial Population of Filaments PA in the Galactic Plane" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                - generic [ref=e702]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e703]:
                    - text: The most interesting result of our study is the discovery of a new population of short filaments’ PA that is found along the Galactic plane only at
                    - emphasis [ref=e704]: l
                    - text: < 0°. There is statistical evidence that short filaments PA point toward Sgr A* with the cone in which the filaments are found has FWHM ∼ 20°, but the deviations of filament directions from radial is much broader, over a large scale of ∼300 pc from Sgr A* at
                    - emphasis [ref=e705]: l
                    - text: < 0°. This large-scale anisotropy in the filaments PA is interpreted in the context of a large-scale collimated outflow from Sgr A* along the plane. A wind- or jet-driven outflow from Sgr A* has been suggested to explain evidence for outflow in the plane of the Galaxy within a few arcminutes of Sgr A*.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: There are eight different spectroscopic, polarimetric, and broadband continuum measurements over a wide range of angular scales extending from ∼0.02 to ∼25 pc from Sgr A* that have inferred a jet-driven outflow along the Galactic plane (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2012" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib36"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "2020" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                    - text: and references therein). In this picture the jet emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow and is aligned roughly east−west in Galactic coordinates. A schematic diagram in Figure
                    - link "8" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bf8"
                    - text: showing the interaction of the outflow from Sgr A* with filaments of ionized and molecular gas being aligned roughly along the Galactic flow. For example, blue- and redshifted features in radio recombination line observations on a scale within 14″ (0.56 pc) of Sgr A* invoke an interpretation in terms of the interaction of a collimated outflow driven outflow from Sgr A* along ∼ ± 30° of the Galactic plane (Royster et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e710] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                    - text: ). In this picture, the blueshifted arm of the jet emerges to the west of Sgr A* making an angle ∼45° to the line of sight.

              - heading "5. Conclusion" [level=2] [ref=e825]
              - paragraph [ref=e827]:
                - text: In summary, we have presented an analysis of the PA distribution of the entire system of thermal and nonthermal radio filaments in the GC. We use filtered MeerKAT images to determine the PA distributions of the population of nonthermal and thermal radio filaments. We noted alignment of filament directions within 20° of the Galactic plane that suggested a scenario in which a collimated outflow is driven from Sgr A* in the direction along the Galactic plane. The inferred jet is estimated to have a a mass flow rate of 10
                - superscript [ref=e828]: −4
                - emphasis [ref=e829]: M
                - subscript [ref=e830]: ⊙
                - text: yr
                - superscript [ref=e831]: −1
                - text: in order to align nonthermal radio filaments and accelerate thermal gas along the Galactic plane. This outflow emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow of Sgr A* and runs along the Galactic plane. The opening angle of the outflow is estimated to be ∼40° with respect to the Galactic plane where the relativistic jet lies, and the age of the outflow is at least 6 Myr.

              - heading "Abstract" [level=2] [ref=e168]
              - paragraph [ref=e170]:
                - text: We have examined the distribution of the position angle (PA) of the Galactic center filaments with lengths L > 66″ and <66″ as well as their length distribution as a function of PA. We find bimodal PA distributions of the filaments, and long and short populations of radio filaments. Our PA study shows the evidence for a distinct population of short filaments with PA close to the Galactic plane. Mainly thermal, short-radio filaments (<66″) have PAs concentrated close to the Galactic plane within 60° < PA < 120°. Remarkably, the short filament PAs are radial with respect to the Galactic center at l < 0° and extend in the direction toward Sgr A*. On a smaller scale, the prominent Sgr E H ii complex G358.7-0.0 provides a vivid example of the nearly radial distribution of short filaments. The bimodal PA distribution suggests a different origin for two distinct filament populations. We argue that the alignment of the short-filament population results from the ram pressure of a degree-scale outflow from Sgr A* that exceeds the internal filament pressure, and aligns them along the Galactic plane.                     - paragraph [ref=e676]:
                      - text: The dark feature in the continuum MeerKAT and GBT images is anticorrelated with the Sgr E CO cloud. This dark feature shows similar appearance to many GC molecular clouds that have been identified as radio dark clouds (Yusef-Zadeh
                      - link "2012" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:

The deficit of the continuum emission from the volume occupied by molecular gas results in dark features that trace embedded molecular clouds.
              - heading "4. Discussion" [level=2] [ref=e678]
              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively. The vertical and horizontal filaments are characterized to have nonthermal and thermal properties (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ), respectively, based on their spectral indices. While there is clearly an overlap in their properties (e.g., PA, spectral index) a key question is the origin of the bimodal PA distribution of GC filaments.
                - heading "4.1. Vertical Population of Galactic Center Filaments PA" [level=3] [ref=e682]
                - generic [ref=e683]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e684]:
                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north. The negative and positive PAs tend to be found in positive and negative Galactic longitudes, respectively. There is a slightly reduced number of filaments at PAs ∼ 0°, giving roughly a bimodal distribution in the histogram. We also note that vertical filaments dominated by long filaments
                    - emphasis [ref=e685]: L
                    - text: "> 66″ have nonthermal spectra. Considering global distribution of vertical filament PAs, there is no evidence that the extension of all filaments PA converge toward Sgr A* or any other compact sources. This suggests that the creation of roughly symmetric PA distribution is in the Galactic plane within a degree of Sgr A*. This is consistent with a trend noticed in the spectral index of nonthermal filaments as they become steeper with increasing absolute Galactic latitude (Yusef-Zadeh et al."
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ). If synchrotron aging is responsible for the steepening of the spectrum, it implies that the vertical filaments are powered in the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e688]:
                    - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from
                    - text: measurements (e.g., Geballe et al.
                    - link "1999" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib7"
                    - text: ; Oka et al.
                    - link "2005" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib21"
                    - text: ; Oka & Geballe
                    - link "2020" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). The nonthermal radio filaments result from the interaction of the large-scale wind and obstacles embedded within the flow, creating the filaments by wrapping the wind’s magnetic field around the obstacles (Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). However, there are alternate models explaining the origin of the vertical filaments (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ; Sofue
                    - link "2023" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib31"
                    - text: and references therein). This begs the question of the origin of the high cosmic-ray pressure, which is usually attributed to the explosive event a few million years ago that created Fermi bubbles and the bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e699] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ).
                - heading "4.2. Radial Population of Filaments PA in the Galactic Plane" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                - generic [ref=e702]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e703]:
                    - text: The most interesting result of our study is the discovery of a new population of short filaments’ PA that is found along the Galactic plane only at
                    - emphasis [ref=e704]: l
                    - text: < 0°. There is statistical evidence that short filaments PA point toward Sgr A* with the cone in which the filaments are found has FWHM ∼ 20°, but the deviations of filament directions from radial is much broader, over a large scale of ∼300 pc from Sgr A* at
                    - emphasis [ref=e705]: l
                    - text: < 0°. This large-scale anisotropy in the filaments PA is interpreted in the context of a large-scale collimated outflow from Sgr A* along the plane. A wind- or jet-driven outflow from Sgr A* has been suggested to explain evidence for outflow in the plane of the Galaxy within a few arcminutes of Sgr A*.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: There are eight different spectroscopic, polarimetric, and broadband continuum measurements over a wide range of angular scales extending from ∼0.02 to ∼25 pc from Sgr A* that have inferred a jet-driven outflow along the Galactic plane (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2012" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib36"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "2020" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                    - text: and references therein). In this picture the jet emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow and is aligned roughly east−west in Galactic coordinates. A schematic diagram in Figure
                    - link "8" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bf8"
                    - text: showing the interaction of the outflow from Sgr A* with filaments of ionized and molecular gas being aligned roughly along the Galactic flow. For example, blue- and redshifted features in radio recombination line observations on a scale within 14″ (0.56 pc) of Sgr A* invoke an interpretation in terms of the interaction of a collimated outflow driven outflow from Sgr A* along ∼ ± 30° of the Galactic plane (Royster et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e710] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                    - text: ). In this picture, the blueshifted arm of the jet emerges to the west of Sgr A* making an angle ∼45° to the line of sight.

                  - paragraph [ref=e740]: This small-scale geometry of the jet is consistent with our analysis of filaments PA if the two opposing cones of outflowing material are extrapolated to a scale of ∼300 pc. This could be explained by confusion due to crowding of radio continuum features in the inner Galaxy.

                    - text: ). An alternative suggestion that has been put forth is that stretching of molecular gas in Sgr E is due to its motion along
                    - emphasis [ref=e744]: x
                    - text: 1 orbits. The Sgr E complex lies at the intersection of CMZ and the Galactic dust lane, so it is possible that the gravitational potential of the bar is responsible for stretching the Sgr E cloud into filaments (Wallace et al.

                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                    - text: ). This suggestion is based on limited ALMA observations over a small region showing CO filaments on a length scale of 2 pc. It is not clear if this suggestion can explain the radial distribution of filament PAs pointing toward Sgr A* on a scale of 300 pc.

              - heading "5. Conclusion" [level=2] [ref=e825]
              - paragraph [ref=e827]:
                - text: In summary, we have presented an analysis of the PA distribution of the entire system of thermal and nonthermal radio filaments in the GC. We use filtered MeerKAT images to determine the PA distributions of the population of nonthermal and thermal radio filaments. We noted alignment of filament directions within 20° of the Galactic plane that suggested a scenario in which a collimated outflow is driven from Sgr A* in the direction along the Galactic plane. The inferred jet is estimated to have a a mass flow rate of 10
                - superscript [ref=e828]: −4
                - emphasis [ref=e829]: M
                - subscript [ref=e830]: ⊙
                - text: yr
                - superscript [ref=e831]: −1
                - text: in order to align nonthermal radio filaments and accelerate thermal gas along the Galactic plane. This outflow emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow of Sgr A* and runs along the Galactic plane. The opening angle of the outflow is estimated to be ∼40° with respect to the Galactic plane where the relativistic jet lies, and the age of the outflow is at least 6 Myr.

              - heading "Abstract" [level=2] [ref=e168]
              - paragraph [ref=e170]:
                - text: We have examined the distribution of the position angle (PA) of the Galactic center filaments with lengths L > 66″ and <66″ as well as their length distribution as a function of PA. We find bimodal PA distributions of the filaments, and long and short populations of radio filaments. Our PA study shows the evidence for a distinct population of short filaments with PA close to the Galactic plane. Mainly thermal, short-radio filaments (<66″) have PAs concentrated close to the Galactic plane within 60° < PA < 120°. Remarkably, the short filament PAs are radial with respect to the Galactic center at l < 0° and extend in the direction toward Sgr A*. On a smaller scale, the prominent Sgr E H ii complex G358.7-0.0 provides a vivid example of the nearly radial distribution of short filaments. The bimodal PA distribution suggests a different origin for two distinct filament populations. We argue that the alignment of the short-filament population results from the ram pressure of a degree-scale outflow from Sgr A* that exceeds the internal filament pressure, and aligns them along the Galactic plane.                   - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA).                     - paragraph [ref=e676]:
                      - text: The dark feature in the continuum MeerKAT and GBT images is anticorrelated with the Sgr E CO cloud. This dark feature shows similar appearance to many GC molecular clouds that have been identified as radio dark clouds (Yusef-Zadeh
                      - link "2012" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:

                      - text: ). We interpret that the dark feature in Sgr E surrounded by compact H ii regions is produced by a deficiency in radio continuum emission from molecular clouds that are embedded in a bath of UV radiation. The deficit of the continuum emission from the volume occupied by molecular gas results in dark features that trace embedded molecular clouds.
              - heading "4. Discussion" [level=2] [ref=e678]
              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively. The vertical and horizontal filaments are characterized to have nonthermal and thermal properties (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ), respectively, based on their spectral indices. While there is clearly an overlap in their properties (e.g., PA, spectral index) a key question is the origin of the bimodal PA distribution of GC filaments.
                - heading "4.1. Vertical Population of Galactic Center Filaments PA" [level=3] [ref=e682]
                - generic [ref=e683]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e684]:
                    - text: One population of filaments has orientations that are vertical to within ∼ ± 25° of the Galactic north. The negative and positive PAs tend to be found in positive and negative Galactic longitudes, respectively. There is a slightly reduced number of filaments at PAs ∼ 0°, giving roughly a bimodal distribution in the histogram. We also note that vertical filaments dominated by long filaments
                    - emphasis [ref=e685]: L
                    - text: "> 66″ have nonthermal spectra. Considering global distribution of vertical filament PAs, there is no evidence that the extension of all filaments PA converge toward Sgr A* or any other compact sources. This suggests that the creation of roughly symmetric PA distribution is in the Galactic plane within a degree of Sgr A*. This is consistent with a trend noticed in the spectral index of nonthermal filaments as they become steeper with increasing absolute Galactic latitude (Yusef-Zadeh et al."
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ). If synchrotron aging is responsible for the steepening of the spectrum, it implies that the vertical filaments are powered in the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e688]:
                    - text: A scenario for the creation of nonthermal radio filaments uses the high cosmic-ray pressure in the GC estimated from
                    - text: measurements (e.g., Geballe et al.
                    - link "1999" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib7"
                    - text: ; Oka et al.
                    - link "2005" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib21"
                    - text: ; Oka & Geballe
                    - link "2020" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                    - text: ). This extreme pressure drives a large-scale wind away from the Galactic plane, creating bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). The nonthermal radio filaments result from the interaction of the large-scale wind and obstacles embedded within the flow, creating the filaments by wrapping the wind’s magnetic field around the obstacles (Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ). However, there are alternate models explaining the origin of the vertical filaments (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2022a" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                    - text: ; Sofue
                    - link "2023" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib31"
                    - text: and references therein). This begs the question of the origin of the high cosmic-ray pressure, which is usually attributed to the explosive event a few million years ago that created Fermi bubbles and the bipolar X-ray and radio emission (Heywood et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                    - text: ; Ponti et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e699] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib22"
                    - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh & Wardle
                    - link "2019" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib44"
                    - text: ).
                - heading "4.2. Radial Population of Filaments PA in the Galactic Plane" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                - generic [ref=e702]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e703]:
                    - text: The most interesting result of our study is the discovery of a new population of short filaments’ PA that is found along the Galactic plane only at
                    - emphasis [ref=e704]: l
                    - text: < 0°. There is statistical evidence that short filaments PA point toward Sgr A* with the cone in which the filaments are found has FWHM ∼ 20°, but the deviations of filament directions from radial is much broader, over a large scale of ∼300 pc from Sgr A* at
                    - emphasis [ref=e705]: l
                    - text: < 0°. This large-scale anisotropy in the filaments PA is interpreted in the context of a large-scale collimated outflow from Sgr A* along the plane. A wind- or jet-driven outflow from Sgr A* has been suggested to explain evidence for outflow in the plane of the Galaxy within a few arcminutes of Sgr A*.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: There are eight different spectroscopic, polarimetric, and broadband continuum measurements over a wide range of angular scales extending from ∼0.02 to ∼25 pc from Sgr A* that have inferred a jet-driven outflow along the Galactic plane (see Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                    - link "2012" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib36"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "2020" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                    - text: and references therein). In this picture the jet emerges perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the accretion flow and is aligned roughly east−west in Galactic coordinates. A schematic diagram in Figure
                    - link "8" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bf8"
                    - text: showing the interaction of the outflow from Sgr A* with filaments of ionized and molecular gas being aligned roughly along the Galactic flow. For example, blue- and redshifted features in radio recombination line observations on a scale within 14″ (0.56 pc) of Sgr A* invoke an interpretation in terms of the interaction of a collimated outflow driven outflow from Sgr A* along ∼ ± 30° of the Galactic plane (Royster et al.
                    - link "2019" [ref=e710] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                    - text: ). In this picture, the blueshifted arm of the jet emerges to the west of Sgr A* making an angle ∼45° to the line of sight.

                    - text: ). This suggestion is based on limited ALMA observations over a small region showing CO filaments on a length scale of 2 pc. It is not clear if this suggestion can explain the radial distribution of filament PAs pointing toward Sgr A* on a scale of 300 pc.

              - heading "5. Conclusion" [level=2] [ref=e825]
              - paragraph [ref=e827]:
                - text: In summary, we have presented an analysis of the PA distribution of the entire system of thermal and nonthermal radio filaments in the GC. We use filtered MeerKAT images to determine the PA distributions of the population of nonthermal and thermal radio filaments. We noted alignment of filament directions within 20° of the Galactic plane that suggested a scenario in which a collimated outflow is driven from Sgr A* in the direction along the Galactic plane. The inferred jet is estimated to have a a mass flow rate of 10

The opening angle of the outflow is estimated to be ∼40° with respect to the Galactic plane where the relativistic jet lies, and the age of the outflow is at least 6 Myr.

              - heading "1. Introduction" [level=2] [ref=e202]
              - generic [ref=e203]:
                - paragraph [ref=e204]:
                  - text: The prototype magnetized radio filaments in the Galactic center (GC) were discovered close to 40 years ago (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "1984" [ref=e205] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib42"
                  - text: ). Since then, Very Large Array (VLA), Nobeyama 45m-telescope, Mologlo, and ATCA observations have shown linearly polarized synchrotron emission tracing nucleus-wide cosmic-ray activity throughout the inner few hundred parsecs of the Galaxy (Liszt
                  - link "1985" [ref=e206] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib17"
                  - text: ; Bally & Yusef-Zadeh
                  - link "1989" [ref=e207] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - link "1999" [ref=e210] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib13"
                  - text: ; Reich et al.
                  - link "2000" [ref=e211] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib25"
                  - text: ; Nord et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e212] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib19"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e213] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib41"
                  - text: ; LaRosa et al.
                  - link "2005" [ref=e214] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: ; Law et al.
                  - link "2008" [ref=e215] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: ; Pound & Yusef-Zadeh
                  - link "2018" [ref=e216] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib23"
                  - text: ; Arendt et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e217] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib2"
                  - text: ; Staguhn et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e218] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib33"
                  - text: ). Chandra, XMM-Newton (XMM), and NuSTAR have also detected X-ray emission from a handful of nonthermal radio filaments. (Lu et al.
                  - link "2003" [ref=e219] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib18"
                  - text: ; Sakano et al.
                  - link "2003" [ref=e220] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib28"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2005" [ref=e221] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib46"
                  - text: ; Zhang et al.
                  - link "2014" [ref=e222] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib47"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2020" [ref=e223] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib48"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e224] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib45"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e225]:
                  - text: High-temperature molecular clouds with large, turbulent line widths also characterize this region, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). Furthermore,
                  - generic [ref=e228]:
                    - generic [ref=e230]:
                      - generic [ref=e235]: H
                      - generic [ref=e236]:
                        - generic [ref=e239]: +
                        - generic [ref=e242]: "3"
                    - math [ref=e244]:
                      - generic [ref=e245]:
                        - generic [ref=e249]: H
                        - generic [ref=e251]: "3"
                        - generic [ref=e253]: +
                  - text: absorption line observations show that high cosmic-ray ionization rates permeate the CMZ at levels 1000 times that of the solar neighborhood (Oka & Geballe
                  - link "2020" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib20"
                  - text: ). These observations indicate that cosmic-ray pressure in the CMZ is significant when compared to the interstellar gas pressure of the GC.
                - paragraph [ref=e255]:
                  - text: Recent MeerKAT observations have provided a remarkable mosaic of the inner few degrees of the GC with exquisite details at 4″–6″ spatial resolution (Heywood et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib12"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib11"
                  - text: ). Statistical properties of the population of GC filaments such as morphology, mean spectral index, equipartition magnetic field, filament spacing and filament association with stellar candidates have recently been studied in detail in a series of papers (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022a" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib37"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022b" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib38"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2022c" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib40"
                  - text: ). VLA observations showed the bright and long filaments emitting nonthermal emission, whereas MeerKAT data showed a great deal of fainter filaments and filamentary structures that are shorter. MeerKAT has also surveyed a large number of galaxy clusters, some of which show exceptional isolated filamentary structures in the intracluster medium (ICM). These filaments appear to be linked to radio jets, tails, and lobes of radio galaxies (Shimwell et al.
                  - link "2016" [ref=e261] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib30"
                  - text: ; Ramatsoku et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib24"
                  - text: ; Condon et al.
                  - link "2021" [ref=e263] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib5"
                  - text: ; Rudnick et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib27"
                  - text: ). For the first time, a population of magnetized ICM filaments, with an underlying physical mechanism similar to that of the GC filament population, is identified in external galaxies (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2022d" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib39"
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=e266]:
                  - text: With the new and sensitive MeerKAT images of the Galactic center (GC), we continue examining the physical properties of the GC filaments, focusing on their position angle (PA). This physical characteristic could potentially provide additional insight into the origin of the enigmatic GC filaments. Previous VLA observations of the brightest GC filaments showed that they are mainly oriented perpendicular to the Galactic plane (Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2004" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib41"
                  - text: and references therein). Using the high sensitivity of MeerKAT data, we examine statistical properties of the PA of the GC filament population. We present evidence that short filaments located on the negative Galactic longitudes have PAs that run mainly within ±20° of the Galactic plane. An extension of the filament PAs show radial distribution, pointing in the direction toward Sgr A* at the GC. The orientation of a large number of filaments within a few hundred parsecs of Sgr A* is similar to those found in radio continuum and recombination line images of the inner few arcminutes of Sgr A* (Royster et al.
                  - link "2019" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib26"
                  - text: ; Yusef-Zadeh et al.
                  - link "2020" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib43"
                  - text: ). In addition, ALMA observations of the Sgr E molecular cloud shows parallel filamentary structure along the Galactic plane (Wallace et al.
                  - link "2022" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#apjlacd54bbib34"
                  - text: ). Here we consider a picture in which a collimated outflow, most likely arising from Sgr A*, is responsible for distorting and aligning the shape of molecular, thermal, and nonthermal features along the Galactic plane.

              - generic [ref=e679]:
                - paragraph [ref=e680]:
                  - text: Our analysis of the GC filaments’ PA distribution indicate two different filament populations. The PAs of the long and short filaments tend to lie in the directions perpendicular and parallel to the Galactic plane, respectively.
